titulo: Real estate as investment: the premise the data doesn't support

corpo:
Real estate holds a singular position in Brazilian financial culture. It is treated as the store of value par excellence, a tangible asset that withstands crises, generates income, and appreciates over time. This conviction crosses generations and levels of financial sophistication. That is exactly why it deserves rigorous examination.

The premise has legitimate historical roots in a country that experienced hyperinflation, savings confiscation, and chronic monetary instability. The problem is that it survived the context that justified it. Today it operates as bias, not as analysis.

The anatomy of any income-producing asset

Every income-producing asset has two components: a principal, which needs to preserve value over time, and a periodic income, which compensates the capital while it is committed.

With real estate, the principal is the value of the property. What determines its variation is not an inflation index, but variables specific to the real estate market: location, supply and demand, credit availability, interest rate levels, and regional infrastructure. FipeZAP consolidates the outcome of these forces into an observable index — it measures what the market actually practiced, not a correction contractually guaranteed by any index. Rent is the periodic income, paid monthly by the tenant.

The Brazilian capital markets offer an asset class with a superficially similar structure, but with a fundamental difference: federal government bonds linked to the IPCA have their Updated Nominal Value adjusted daily by the official index, by contract, without depending on any market variable. The periodic income is the coupon, paid at a frequency that varies by bond. The entry cost is close to zero.

This distinction is not cosmetic. With real estate, preservation of the principal depends on forces the investor does not control and that bear no direct relationship to inflation. With the NTN-B, correction of the principal is a contractual obligation of the National Treasury, calculated on the official IPCA from IBGE, independent of any market condition. This analysis sets both sides of the equation on the same criteria.

What you pay before you even start

Whoever buys a R$500,000 property commits, in practice, R$542,500.

  • ITBI (3%): R$15,000

  • Brokerage (5%): R$25,000

  • Notary and registration (0.5%): R$2,500

Total entry friction: R$42,500, equivalent to 8.5% of the asset. That money does not earn a return, does not come back, and does not compound. The property starts 8.5% below the starting point before any return is generated. With IPCA-linked government bonds, the entry cost is close to zero.

Source: municipal ITBI tables, average of Brazilian state capitals.

The income that rent actually delivers

FipeZAP points to an annualized residential rental yield of 6.2% in February 2026. On R$500,000, that represents R$31,000 gross per year. That number does not reach the investor's pocket.

Historical average vacancy is 10% of the period. Net of that, effective rent falls to R$27,900. Average property tax (IPTU): 0.5% of value, R$2,500 annually. Conservative maintenance: another 0.5%, R$2,500. The result before income tax is R$22,900 annually, R$1,908 per month. With income tax under the progressive table, estimated effective rate of 15%: another R$3,435 goes out.

  • Net income in the first year: R$19,465, equivalent to R$1,622 per month.

  • Net yield on committed capital (R$542,500): 3.59% per year.

The government bond with semiannual coupons linked to IPCA, traded on April 10, 2026 at IPCA + 7.34%, delivers a tax-free coupon of R$2,125 per month over the same period, with initial capital R$42,500 lower and zero active management. Thirty-one percent more net income from the very first month.

By 2036, with the Updated Nominal Value growing 4.5% per year via IPCA, the bond's monthly net coupon reaches R$3,300. The property's net rent, whose price moved according to the real estate market's own dynamics at a CAGR of 3.5% per year over the last ten years, reaches, after all costs, R$2,288. The bond's advantage increases over time.

Source: FipeZAP — National residential index, Feb. 2026; Tesouro Direto — rates as of April 10, 2026.

The retirement that real estate promises

The second most common use of real estate as an investment is building future income. You buy today to rent out in ten or fifteen years. The Brazilian capital markets have an instrument designed precisely for this: Tesouro Renda+.

Calculation memo — bond for future income (IPCA + 7.11%), 10 years of accumulation:

  • Nominal return: (1 + 7.11%) × (1 + 4.5%) − 1 = 11.93% per year

  • Capital accumulated by 2036: R$500,000 × (1.1193)^10 = R$1,543,239

  • Gross monthly income: R$11,861

  • After 15% income tax: R$10,082/month net, adjusted by IPCA, for 20 years.

An important structural point: Renda+ does not return the principal as a lump sum at the end. Each monthly installment includes real interest plus principal amortization — it is an annuity. At the end of the 240 months, the balance is zero. The total net amount received over the 20 years is R$2,419,740, which incorporates the full return of the accumulated capital of R$1,543,239 plus the real interest of the period.

Real estate under the same conditions delivers in 2036, after vacancy, costs, and income tax, considering that its value evolved according to real estate market variables as consolidated by FipeZAP: R$2,288/month.

Four point four times less monthly income. With active management, vacancy risk, and zero guarantee of cash flow.

Source: Tesouro Direto — Renda+ 2036, rate as of April 10, 2026; FipeZAP — national historical series.

Pure accumulation

For those who don't need income during the period and want to maximize wealth in ten years:

Real estate:

  • Committed capital: R$542,500

  • Net value in 2036: R$674,504 (CAGR of 3.5% p.a., the result of market dynamics via FipeZAP, after income tax).

  • Net accumulated income (10 years): R$194,650

  • Total wealth: R$869,154 | Real IRR: 0.94% per year

Principal government bond (IPCA + 7.11%):

  • Capital: R$500,000

  • Gross value in 2036: R$1,543,239

  • After 15% income tax and B3 custody fees: R$1,374,753 | Real CAGR: 5.88% per year

The bond adjusts the principal daily by IPCA, by contract. Real estate appreciates according to market variables — credit, demand, location, the Selic rate — with no guarantee of outcome whatsoever. Over the last ten years, the result of these variables, as measured by FipeZAP, was 3.5% per year nominal, below inflation for the period.

The final wealth of the investor in the IPCA+ bond is 58% higher, with initial capital R$42,500 lower.

Source: FipeZAP — residential CAGR over the last 10 years, national index; Tesouro Direto — NTN-B Principal 2040, rate as of April 10, 2026.

Summary

Assumptions: IPCA 4.5% per year (top of the target range, consistent with the neutral rate declared by the BCB); real estate CAGR 3.5% nominal (FipeZAP, last 10 years — the result of the real estate market's own dynamics, not IPCA indexation); rental yield 6.2% (FipeZAP, Feb. 2026); government bond rates as of April 10, 2026; 15% income tax in all cases.

What the statement doesn't show

The numbers answer the return. They don't explain why real estate persists as the dominant choice even with a systematic disadvantage in the data. The answer lies in how often the risk is observed.

1. Volatility and the Pain of Loss: Long-term government bonds have high duration. When rates rise, market price falls. In 2024, portfolios with long IPCA+ bonds posted declines of 20% or more. Kahneman and Tversky showed that the pain of a loss is roughly twice the satisfaction of a gain. The investor sees it, feels it, and sells at the worst moment. Real estate does not produce this signal. In 2015-2017, FipeZAP recorded a nominal decline, but no statement ever notified the investor. The risk was present; what differed was the frequency of measurement.

2. The Illusion of Control: The real estate investor feels in control (renovation, rent, tenant). With bonds, the perception is one of passivity in the face of Copom decisions. The illusion of control has real psychological value, but it costs 4.94 percentage points per year in sacrificed real return.

3. Return Risk vs. Exit Risk: A government bond held to maturity has no return risk. Whoever locks in IPCA + 7.11% today and holds the bond receives exactly that. Real estate never offers that guarantee. Its value at sale depends on interest rates, credit, and local dynamics — variables the investor does not control and that FipeZAP only records ex-post.

When real estate makes sense

This analysis does not condemn real estate as an asset class, but it does delimit the context in which it is justified:

  • When there is a local information advantage that the average index does not capture (anticipated demand vectors).

  • Acquisition below market value (auctions, distressed sales, or off-plan purchases with a real discount).

  • Value-add strategies, where the return comes from the ability to add something the market has not yet priced in.

  • When personal use justifies the asset regardless of pure financial return.

The case that does not hold up is the most common one: buying a standard residential property to rent out, convinced that the asset will "track inflation" through some intrinsic property. It won't. The real estate market (credit, interest rates, supply) will determine the outcome. And over the last ten years, that outcome, as consolidated by FipeZAP, came in below the IPCA in real terms.

Choosing real estate with clear-eyed awareness of these numbers is a legitimate decision. Recognizing psychological and inheritance-related factors is different from ignoring the numbers. A conscious choice presupposes knowing the cost of what one is choosing.

Sources:

  • FipeZAP — Residential Property Price Index, national historical series, Jan. 2008 to Mar. 2026 (FIPE/ZAP Imóveis).

  • Tesouro Direto — IPCA+ bond rates, consulted on April 10, 2026.

  • BCB — Focus Report and communications on the structural neutral interest rate.

  • Kahneman, D. & Tversky, A. (1979). Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk.

  • FipeZAP — April 2025 and December 2024 reports (FIPE/OLX Group).
